factoids.name: Earth's Terminator Line
factoids.text:
earth's terminator line the earth's terminator line (also called the "grey line" or "twilight zone") is the moving boundary that separates the illuminated day side from the dark night side of the planet. as the earth rotates eastward, this line sweeps across the globe, bringing sunrise to one side and sunset to the exact opposite. it is not a sharp line: because the atmosphere bends (refracts) sunlight, the terminator is a fuzzy band about 37 miles (60 km) wide.

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/terminator_(solar))

factoids.name: The origin of the word "gentleman"
factoids.text:
the origin of the word "gentleman" "gentleman" originates from the middle english gentilman and old french gentilhomme, tracing back to latin gentilis ("of the same family/clan") and homo ("man"). dating to the 13th century, it originally meant a man of noble birth, high social standing, or one entitled to bear arms, evolving over time to denote polite, well-bred behaviour. the focus shifted from birthright to character, and today it rarely refers to inherited status. the word "gentle" here does not mean "mild" but rather "well-born" (from gentil).

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/gentleman)

factoids.name: What are orchids anyway?
factoids.text:
what are orchids anyway? yes, orchids are flowers. specifically, they are a vast and diverse family of flowering plants known as orchidaceae, comprising over 25,000 to 30,000 species worldwide. orchids are highly specialized, often colorful, and are considered angiosperms, meaning they produce seeds. they are found on every continent except antarctica. orchid flowers have a highly specialized, bilaterally symmetrical structure, often featuring a modified petal called a labellum or lip. unlike most flowers, orchids have a central column where the male (stamen) and female (pistil) reproductive parts are fused together. they are not just flowers in the general sense but are technically classified as one of the most advanced and diverse groups of flowering plants.

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/orchid)

factoids.name: When was the first jigsaw invented?
factoids.text:
when was the first jigsaw invented? the first jigsaw puzzle was invented around 1760-1767 by john spilsbury, a london cartographer and engraver. he created it by mounting a map onto wood and cutting along the country borders to create an educational tool for teaching geography to children. they were initially called "dissected maps" or "dissections" and were designed to teach children geography, featuring maps of europe and the world. the first puzzles were made of mahogany or other hardwood. in the 1880s, the invention of the fretsaw allowed more precise, intricate cuts, leading to the term "jigsaw" puzzle. cardboard puzzles were introduced in the late 1800s but did not become widespread until the 1930s, when they became popular as an affordable, calming activity during the great depression.

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/jigsaw_puzzle)

factoids.name: Apex predator
factoids.text:
apex predator an apex predator is a carnivore at the top of its food chain, with no natural predators as an adult, that controls prey populations and plays a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem balance. they occupy the highest trophic level, with examples like lions, orcas, great white sharks, and polar bears. by regulating prey numbers, they prevent overgrazing and maintain the health of other species, preventing ecosystem collapse. a classic example: when wolves (apex predators) were removed from yellowstone, elk populations exploded, leading to overgrazing of willow and aspen trees; reintroducing wolves helped restore balance by controlling elk numbers.

factoids.name: Tying shoelaces is a complex task for humanoid robot
factoids.text:
tying shoelaces is a complex task for humanoid robot yes, tying shoelaces has traditionally been an extremely complex and challenging task for robots. while humans learn this fine motor skill as children, the task breaks many assumptions of traditional robotics and has served as a benchmark challenge in ai and dexterous manipulation. the difficulty stems from: deformable objects (shoelaces are soft, dynamic, and flexible, hard to model with traditional rigid-body methods); dexterity and finesse (tying a knot requires fine finger dexterity, tactile sensing, and gentle tension control); complex dynamics (a slight imprecision may require restarting the whole long-horizon, multi-step process); and variability (laces and shoes vary greatly). recent breakthroughs by companies like google deepmind, using advanced ai systems such as aloha unleashed and demostart, have allowed robots to learn this task from human demonstrations via imitation learning, large-scale data collection, and diffusion models enabling bimanual (two-armed) manipulation.

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/moravec%27s_paradox)

factoids.name: Why Logarithms?
factoids.text:
why logarithms? logarithms are used to solve exponential equations, calculate compound interest, and measure quantities that span a very large range of values on a logarithmic scale — like sound intensity (decibels) or the strength of an earthquake (richter scale). they're also useful across computer science, finance, chemistry, and physics for analysing growth rates, data compression, and radioactive decay. a few uses: solving exponential equations (logs are the inverse of exponents, so they find unknown exponents — e.g. how long an investment takes to reach a certain value); compressing wide ranges (on the decibel scale a 10 db increase is 10× louder and 20 db is 100×; the richter scale measures earthquake magnitude); modelling growth and decay (population growth, radiocarbon dating); and in computing, data compression and information theory (the number of bits needed to store a value).

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/logarithm)

factoids.name: Priest cannot testify against parishioner even if they confessed to a crime such as homicide in USA and India
factoids.text:
priest cannot testify against parishioner even if they confessed to a crime such as homicide in usa and india in the usa, a confession of murder made to a priest during the sacrament of reconciliation is generally not admissible in court, under the “priest–penitent privilege” recognised in all 50 states (and many other countries) to protect the confidentiality of communications between clergy and those seeking spiritual counsel. under canon law the “seal of confession” is absolute and inviolable — a priest who reveals anything from a confession faces automatic excommunication, and priests are expected to go to prison rather than break it. the privilege applies only to communication meant to be confidential for spiritual guidance; some jurisdictions carve out exceptions (e.g. mandatory reporting of child abuse), and a statement made informally outside the sacrament is generally not protected.

in india, such a confession is also generally inadmissible, but for a different reason: it is treated as an extra-judicial confession — considered weak evidence that requires independent corroboration. under the indian evidence act a confession is admissible only if voluntary, and courts regard extra-judicial confessions as unreliable, requiring corroborating evidence before relying on one.

[read more on wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/priest%e2%80%93penitent_privilege)

factoids.name: Language related shortcuts
factoids.text:
language related shortcuts - maxim - a general truth or rule of conduct, usually formal or philosophical (“know thyself”)
- proverb - a short, traditional saying stating a general truth or advice (“a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush”)
- allegory - an extended story where characters/events symbolize deeper meanings (animal farm representing the russian revolution)
- parallel - a comparison showing similarity between two things to clarify or prove a point (“this situation parallels the 2008 financial crisis”)
- analogy - explaining something unfamiliar by comparing it to something familiar (“the heart pumps blood like a water pump moves water through pipes”)
- metaphor - direct comparison (“time is money”)
- simile - comparison using “like” or “as” (“brave as a lion”)
- parable - short story teaching a moral lesson
- fable - fictional tale, often with animals, conveying a lesson
- adage - old, well-known saying expressing common experience
- aphorism - concise statement of truth or principle
- idiom - phrase whose meaning isn’t literal (“kick the bucket”)
- trope - recurring theme or device
- archetype - universal character type or situation (the hero’s journey)
- exemplum - illustrative example or anecdote proving a point
- denouement - an element in the structure of a story, in which all plot lines typically come to a resolution, events are explained, etc. it usually follows the climax. the term is borrowed from the french word dénouement derived from old french desnouer, 'to untie', which is from latin: nodus, 'knot'.

factoids.name: Literary Canon
factoids.text:
literary canon literary canon is a collection of works, such as books, poems, and plays, that are considered the most significant and influential within a culture. these texts are recognized for their enduring stylistic quality, social or intellectual value, and impact on later works and writers. the canon serves as a benchmark for literary excellence but is also a subject of debate, as it has historically faced criticism for being narrow and has been broadened over time to include more diverse voices.

key characteristics
- **significance**: works in the canon are seen as masterpieces that have shaped literature and thought.
- **influence**: they have influenced subsequent writers and genres, and can shape a culture's understanding of itself.
- **timelessness**: canonical works are often those that remain relevant across centuries.
- **consensus**: inclusion is based on a consensus among scholars, critics, and educators regarding the work's quality and importance.
- **dynamic**: the canon is not static and changes over time to reflect evolving societal values, leading to the inclusion of works from more diverse backgrounds.

examples
- **the western canon**: often associated with works by authors like william shakespeare, jane austen, and homer.
- **expanded canon**: contemporary movements have expanded the canon to include writers like toni morrison and gabriel garcia marquez.

factoids.name: Why is rape seed called so?
factoids.text:

factoids.name: Does a passenger aeroplane have a morgue?
factoids.text:
does a passenger aeroplane have a morgue? no — commercial passenger flights don't have a dedicated morgue. if someone dies in flight, the body is typically moved to an empty seat or row when available and covered with a blanket; otherwise it stays in the person's own seat, handled as dignifiedly as space allows. one historical exception: some long-haul aircraft, such as the singapore airlines airbus a340-500, had a special body compartment — sometimes nicknamed a “corpse cupboard” — fitted with straps and used only when no other suitable space was available. but that was a rare feature, not a standard morgue.

factoids.name: Why is left wing called left wing?
factoids.text:
why is left wing called left wing? the terms "left wing" and "right wing" in politics come from the physical seating arrangement in the french national assembly during the french revolution in the late 1700s.
when the assembly met, supporters of the king and the old aristocratic order sat on the right side of the chamber, while those who favored revolution and change sat on the left side. this wasn't planned as political symbolism - it likely happened somewhat naturally as like-minded delegates gravitated toward each other.
the "left" represented those pushing for radical change: overthrowing the monarchy, reducing the power of the church, and creating a more egalitarian society. the "right" represented those wanting to preserve traditional institutions and hierarchies.
this seating arrangement became so associated with different political philosophies that the terms stuck. over time, "left wing" came to describe political positions that generally favor social change, equality, and progressive reforms, while "right wing" describes positions that tend to favor tradition, established institutions, and gradual rather than radical change.
it's quite remarkable how a simple matter of where people chose to sit in one room over 200 years ago gave us the political vocabulary we still use today to describe the entire spectrum of political thought worldwide.
